previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of dilated cardiomyopathy, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, diabetes, and prior stroke was admitted for acute worsening of shortness of breath and leg swelling. The exacerbation was due to accidentally missing five days of Lasix after mistakenly refilling metoprolol instead. He received IV diuresis with significant fluid removal and improvement in symptoms. His INR was supratherapeutic (peaking at 3.9), so warfarin was held. He was transitioned from Lasix to torsemide 40mg daily, and discharge instructions emphasized daily weight monitoring and outpatient INR follow-up. He was discharged stable, with improved edema and respiratory status.

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ is a ___ gentleman with a history of systolic 
CHF, DM II, and atrial fib/flutter on coumadin who presented 
with volume overload and bilateral lower extremity edema of two 
weeks' duration in the setting of increased salt intake. He was 
admitted for wound care and diuresis. Unfortunately, he elected 
to leave the hospital on the day after admission in spite of 
ongoing volume overload. 

ACTIVE ISSUES

1. Lower extremity ulcers: Patient's ulcers developed fairly 
suddenly in the setting of volume overload. He had had no frank 
pain, though he has decreased sensation in the setting of 
neuropathy. None of his ulcers probed to bone and inflammatory 
markers were only mildly elevated, making osteomyelitis less 
likely. Although several ulcers had a small margin of erythema, 
this was most consistent with hyperemia and not cellulitis. 
There were no symptoms of systemic infection and WBC was normal. 
Thus, patient was not started on antibiotics. Podiatry was 
consulted and did not feel lesions needed debridement. They 
recommended lac-hydrin cream, dry dressing to decrease the 
chances of superinfection. Peripheral edema had begun to improve 
slightly on day #2 of admission after 80 mg PO torsemide on 
___ and 200 mg IV furosemide on the morning of ___. Team 
planned for repeat electrolytes followed by a second dose of 
furosemide on the afternoon of ___. However, patient elected to 
leave the hospital in spite of the team's strong recommendation 
that he stay for further diuresis. The risk of worsening ulcers, 
poor wound healing, and possible amputation were discussed with 
patient explicitly and he expressed understanding. He decided to 
leave the hospital. 

2. Acute on Chronic Systolic CHF: LVEF ___ in ___. Patient 
has refused evaluation for ICD for primary prevention in the 
past. He presented with worsening shortness of breath/edema 
which was likely secondary to decompensated CHF in the setting 
of dietary indiscretion. He was continued on home doses of 
ramipril and spironolactone. He refused a CXR. He needed 
aggressive diuresis. We gave home dose of 80 mg torsemide on 
evening of arrival (while waiting for electrolyte panel) to good 
effect (-8lb in 12 hours)and then begun IV diuresis with 200 mg 
IV furosemide on morning of ___. Patient continued to have 
significant volume overload and needed further diuresis; 
however, he elected to leave the hospital as above. He refused 
to stay for planned 3pm electrolyte check. Risk of worsening 
heart failure, respiratory failure, and even death if patient 
does not adhere to heart failure regimen were discussed 
explicitly and patient voiced understanding. 

3. Diabetes: Patient reported his home regimen is 45 units NPH 
in the morning and another 45 units at bedtime if finger stick 
is > 130. However, it was not clear how often he actually takes 
insulin. Last A1C 7.9% on ___. Given uncertainties about 
patient's home dose, NPH was started at 20 units NPH BID with 
ISS and with plans to uptitrate according to total daily insulin 
requirements. Unfortunately, patient left the hospital before 
dose adjustments could be made. 

CHRONIC ISSUES: 

1. History of CVA: Continued ASA 325 mg daily

2. Constipation: Continued lactulose PRN

3. Paroxysmal Atrial Fibrillation/Flutter: Patient has a history 
of non-compliance with INR checks but was therapeutic at recent 
visit. Continued warfarin 5 mg PO daily. Continued metoprolol 
succinate 25 mg daily.

4. High Cholesterol: Continued Pravastatin

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___, 

It was a pleasure caring for you during your admission to ___. 
As you know, you were admitted with fluid overload and ulcers on 
your legs and feet. Your fluid overload is most likely related 
to your heart failure. We began treatment with intravenous 
lasix.

Rather than stay for additional treatment, you decided to leave 
the hospital. We explained our strong recommendation that you 
stay in the hospital for further diuresis in order to improve 
your shortness of breath and give your ulcers the best chance of 
healing. We explained the risk of worsening fluid overload, 
including non-healing ulcers, amputation, respiratory failure, 
and even possibly death if you do not treat your heart failure. 
You understood these risks and decided to leave the hospital. 

We are discharging you with a refill for torsemide 80 mg daily. 
We strongly recommend that you call your PCP, ___, 
and your Podiatrist on ___ to set up follow-up appointments 
in the next week. Please also weigh yourself every morning and 
call your doctor if your weight goes up by more than 3 lbs.

Please also keep your ulcers clean and wrapped in dry gauze to 
prevent infection. We also recommend using lac-hydrin cream on 
your legs and feet. If you develop fevers, chills, worsening 
pain, or pus coming out of your ulcer, it could be a sign of a 
serious infection and it is very important that you call your 
doctor or go to the Emergency Department.
